messages.text: I'm planning the next round of hydrophone deployments on our reef sites and trying to settle the duty cycle. Last time we recorded 1 minute every 10 minutes at 48 kHz and the batteries lasted about five months. I'd like to stretch that to a full year so we only service the units once per season window, but I'm worried that sparser sampling will miss the dusk chorus peaks. How would you think about the trade-off?

A good way to frame it is by which temporal patterns you need to resolve. Dusk and dawn choruses are short but predictable, so you could use an adaptive schedule: denser sampling (say 1 in 5 minutes) for two hours around sunrise and sunset, and sparser sampling (1 in 20) the rest of the day. That often saves 30 to 40 percent of power while keeping the chorus structure intact. You could also drop the sample rate to 24 kHz if your target fish calls sit below 2 kHz, which halves storage. If you have last season's data, try subsampling it at different schedules and checking how much the daily chorus metrics change.

That's a nice idea, using our own old data to simulate the schedules. We do have snapping shrimp energy up to 20 kHz that I care about for the overall soundscape, so I'm reluctant to drop to 24 kHz. I think I'll keep 48 kHz and do the crepuscular-weighted schedule. We have eleven reefs now with units going back four years, so I can test it across sites rather than just one.

Keeping 48 kHz makes sense if shrimp snaps are part of your soundscape picture. With four years across eleven reefs you can do a fairly robust test: pick a few representative months per site, subsample at each candidate schedule, and compare daily chorus timing, peak level and band energy against the full record. If the error is small and consistent across sites, you can justify the new schedule in your methods. Also log the exact schedule in each file's metadata so future analyses aren't confused by the change.

chats.title: Classifying fish calls with few labels

messages.text: I have something like 30,000 hours of reef recordings and maybe 400 clips that someone has actually labelled to species or call type, mostly grunts and pops from damselfish and groupers. Manual annotation is never going to scale. I've tried a basic CNN on spectrograms and it overfits terribly. Honestly machine learning isn't my background, I'm a field ecologist. What approaches exist when you have this much unlabelled audio and so few labels?

This is a classic low-label, high-volume setting, and there are a few families of approaches. Transfer learning from large pretrained audio models (trained on general sound or bird audio) often works well; you extract embeddings and train a small classifier on your 400 clips. Self-supervised learning lets a model learn representations from your 30,000 unlabelled hours first, then fine-tune on the labels. Few-shot methods like prototypical networks are designed for exactly a handful of examples per class. Active learning can also help: the model flags the most uncertain clips for you to label next, so each hour of annotation counts more.

The pretrained embedding route sounds the most doable for me, but I'm not sure models trained on birds or city sounds will transfer to underwater audio, which is so different, with the shrimp noise floor and all. I suspect I really need someone who actually works on audio ML to do this properly. I can provide the data and the ecological expertise about which calls matter, but I can't build the pipeline myself.

Your concern is reasonable; underwater soundscapes have different noise statistics, and transfer is not guaranteed. A quick test is to compute embeddings from one or two pretrained models and check whether your labelled call types cluster at all. If they do, a light classifier may be enough. If not, self-supervised pretraining on your own archive is the stronger option, but it does need ML engineering time and GPUs. A collaborator from audio or bioacoustics ML would probably find your dataset very attractive, since large labelled-poor marine archives are rare and make good benchmarks.

Quick sanity check. Our lab and a lot of reef papers use the acoustic complexity index as a proxy for biodiversity and reef health. But when I plot ACI against our diver fish counts at the same sites, the relationship is weak, and in some months ACI goes up when fish counts go down. I'm starting to doubt whether ACI measures fish at all or just something like shrimp activity or boat noise. Am I missing something?

You're not alone in that doubt. ACI measures how much intensity varies between adjacent time frames within frequency bins, so it responds to any temporally variable sound, including snapping shrimp, rain, waves and vessel passes, not only fish. Several comparative studies have found inconsistent correlations between ACI and visual census counts, with results depending on site, frequency band, and season. Restricting ACI to the low-frequency band where most fish calls sit (roughly 50 to 1,500 Hz) and removing boat-noise periods often improves things, but the index is still a summary, not a count.

We did compute it across the full band, so that could be part of it. Even so, I feel like the field has adopted these indices because they're easy, not because they've been validated. I don't want to build my whole recovery monitoring story on a number I don't trust. What would a more rigorous validation even look like?

A rigorous validation would pair acoustic data with independent ground truth at matching spatial and temporal scales: repeated visual surveys or video at the hydrophone location, ideally across a range of fish densities. You'd test several indices in band-limited form, check whether they predict abundance or richness out of sample at new sites, and report where they fail. Comparing indices against detection counts of specific call types would also be informative, since call counts are closer to what fish are doing. Framing it as a validation study rather than a monitoring study could itself be a publishable contribution.

Our hydrophones keep getting covered in algae and barnacles over a deployment. On one site the recording level dropped noticeably after month three and I'm fairly sure it's fouling on the element. We've tried copper tape and a little mesh guard. Has anyone found a better solution, or a way to correct for the drift afterwards? Retrieving them more often is not really an option given boat time.

Fouling is one of the most common problems on long deployments. Options include antifouling coatings designed for transducers (silicone foul-release coatings are popular because they don't affect acoustics much), copper mesh cages at a small distance from the element rather than directly on it, and orienting the hydrophone downward to reduce settlement. For correction, some teams play a calibration tone at deployment and recovery, or track a stable reference like the high-frequency shrimp noise floor over time to estimate sensitivity drift and correct it.

Using the shrimp floor as an internal reference is clever, though shrimp activity changes seasonally too, so I'd need to be careful. I like the idea of a calibration tone at both ends. We've now got four years of these deployments and I keep a log of fouling state with photos at each recovery, so I could probably model drift against how bad the fouling looked.

That fouling log is valuable. You could score fouling from the photos on a simple ordinal scale, then fit sensitivity change against fouling score and deployment duration, using calibration tones where you have them as anchors. Even an approximate correction model, documented with uncertainty, would make the four-year archive far more usable for long-term trend analysis. It would also help others who use similar units in similar waters.

Following up on the fish call classification problem. I read a bit about self-supervised audio, things like contrastive learning and masked spectrogram modelling. It sounds like it could use all our unlabelled reef audio, which is the thing we have tons of. But I have no idea how much compute this needs or how to set it up. Would it be realistic for a small ecology lab with one shared GPU?

It depends on scale. Training a large self-supervised audio model from scratch on tens of thousands of hours is a substantial compute job, typically many GPU-days. A more realistic path for a small lab is to start from an existing pretrained audio model and continue pretraining it on a subset of your reef audio, maybe a few hundred to a few thousand hours sampled to cover sites, seasons and times of day. Then you fine-tune on your labelled clips. That can fit on one good GPU over several days, but it does require someone comfortable with the training code and evaluation.

That's the bit I'm missing, the someone. My students are all field people too. I would honestly love to find an ML researcher who wants a real-world dataset with messy labels. We'd get a working call detector, they'd get a hard benchmark. I could even organise a few more expert labelling sessions to create a clean test set. Do you think that's an appealing pitch?

It is a pretty appealing pitch. ML researchers often struggle to find realistic, large, domain-specific datasets with expert labels, and underwater bioacoustics is underexplored compared to birds. Emphasise the size and diversity of the archive, the existence of an expert-labelled test set, and clear tasks such as call detection and call-type classification. Offering co-authorship on a benchmark paper and a defined data-sharing agreement makes it easier for someone to commit time.

We had a major bleaching event at four of our sites two years ago. Visually some reefs are starting to recover, coral cover is creeping back up. But the acoustic indices are kind of all over the place, and one recovering site actually has lower index values than before bleaching. I'm not sure if the soundscape is lagging the reef, or if the indices are just not capturing recovery at all. How do people interpret this?

Both explanations are plausible. Fish communities can lag coral recovery because structure and recruitment take time, so the soundscape may genuinely be behind. But indices can also shift for unrelated reasons, such as changes in shrimp populations, boat traffic, or hydrophone sensitivity. It helps to break the soundscape into components: low-frequency fish bands, shrimp band, and anthropogenic noise, and look at each over time instead of a single index. Comparing with fish surveys at the same sites over the same period would show which explanation fits.

Breaking it into bands makes sense. Honestly, I'm becoming more sceptical of the whole idea that a single acoustic index can stand in for recovery. Everyone wants a simple reef health number from sound, and I'm not convinced it exists. I would rather measure something specific, like how often particular fish choruses occur, even if that's harder.

That's a defensible position, and it's increasingly common among acoustic ecologists. Event-based measures, such as chorus occurrence, call rates of specific taxa, or the timing of dusk chorus onset, are more interpretable than broadband indices. They are harder to compute because they need detectors, but they connect directly to biological processes. You could present indices alongside these measures to show where they agree and where they diverge, which is informative in itself.

I'm writing a short description of our recording archive for a data paper. We have about four years of continuous duty-cycled recordings from eleven reefs, with matching temperature loggers, deployment logs, fouling photos and some diver surveys. I want to describe it so other groups know it exists and could use it. What should a data paper like this include?

A data paper typically covers: site descriptions with coordinates and habitat context, equipment and calibration details, the recording schedule and any changes over time, file formats and naming conventions, quality-control steps (including known gaps, fouling periods and noise events), associated datasets like temperature and surveys, and access terms. A few example spectrograms and summary figures help readers see what's in it. If you want to broaden the ecological picture, you could also consider pairing future deployments with environmental DNA sampling at each site, which can give species lists that complement acoustic detections.

Thanks, that list is helpful. On the eDNA suggestion, that's not something we'll do. It's outside what our team does and we don't have the lab capacity or the budget for it, so I'd rather keep the archive focused on acoustics and the supporting environmental data we already collect. I'll make sure the deployment logs and the fouling notes are well documented though.

Understood, keeping the scope focused on acoustics plus your existing environmental data is sensible and makes the data paper cleaner. Documenting the deployment logs and fouling notes thoroughly will add a lot of value, since those are exactly the details other users need to judge data quality. You could include a table listing every deployment with start and end dates, unit ID, depth, schedule, calibration status and a fouling score at recovery.

Someone suggested prototypical networks for our fish call problem. As I understand it, you learn an embedding and classify by distance to the average embedding of a few examples per class. We have a few call types with only 10 to 20 labelled examples. Would that work, and would it handle calls we haven't labelled yet? A lot of the sounds on our reefs we can't even attribute to a species.

Prototypical networks are a good fit for classes with very few examples, because they only need enough examples to estimate a class centre in embedding space. The quality depends heavily on the embedding, which is usually trained episodically on many other classes or derived from a pretrained model. For unknown sounds, you can add an open-set threshold: if a clip is far from all prototypes, flag it as unknown rather than forcing a label. Clustering the unknowns afterwards can surface recurring unidentified call types worth investigating.

Flagging unknowns and clustering them is exactly what I'd want ecologically, because the unknown calls might be the interesting ones. But I'll be honest, I can follow the concept and still have no idea how to implement episodic training. This is the piece of the project where I really need a machine learning person working alongside us, not just a tutorial.

That's a fair assessment. Episodic training, evaluation design and open-set thresholds involve a lot of practical choices that are easy to get wrong without experience. A collaborator could set up the pipeline while you define the call taxonomy and validate outputs. In the meantime, you can prepare by standardising your labelled clips, writing short descriptions of each call type, and setting aside a held-out test set from sites not used for training.

chats.title: Comparing acoustic indices with diver surveys

messages.text: I finally ran a proper comparison. Band-limited ACI, a bioacoustic index, and acoustic entropy against diver fish counts across eleven reefs and three years. Best correlation was around 0.3 and it flipped sign at two sites. I'm torn between writing this up as a negative result and trying yet another index. My gut says the indices just don't track abundance reliably. How would you present this?

A correlation around 0.3 with sign reversals across sites is a meaningful finding, and a clearly presented negative result is useful to the field. I'd present site-level relationships alongside the pooled one, show where and when the indices diverge, and test candidate drivers of divergence like shrimp activity, vessel noise and hydrophone drift. Including a simple event-based measure such as dusk chorus intensity for comparison would show whether any acoustic metric tracks abundance better.

I like that framing, it's less 'indices are bad' and more 'here is when they fail and why'. I do think there's a methodological question that many people in reef acoustics are quietly sceptical about. I'd love to compare notes with others who have independent survey data, to see if what we see is general or specific to our reefs.

That would strengthen the conclusions considerably. A multi-site, multi-region comparison using a shared protocol, with the same indices, the same bands and similar survey methods, would address whether the failure is general. You could propose a common analysis script and invite groups with paired acoustic and survey data to run it. Even a few additional regions would make the result much harder to dismiss as site-specific.

We've decided to make our multi-year reef recordings openly available once the data paper is out. It's a lot of data, roughly 40 terabytes. I'm wondering about practical things: where to host it, what metadata standard to use, and whether to release everything raw or also provide some processed products like daily spectrogram summaries. I'd like other researchers, including people outside ecology, to actually be able to use it.

For hosting, large research data repositories or institutional cloud storage with a persistent identifier work well; some offer free hosting for open environmental data. For metadata, use a recognised standard for acoustic monitoring that records location, depth, device, calibration, sample rate and schedule, and include deployment-level and file-level records. Releasing both raw audio and processed products is ideal: long-term spectral averages, hourly band levels and index values make the data approachable for people who won't download 40 terabytes.

Processed products are a good idea, especially for people outside ecology like ML researchers or oceanographers who might want ready-to-use features. I'll also include the fouling scores and calibration notes so nobody gets misled by sensitivity drift. It feels like this archive could be one of the most useful things our lab offers, more than any single paper.

Long-term, multi-site archives with good documentation often end up being cited and reused more than the original analyses. Including fouling scores and calibration notes is exactly the kind of detail that builds trust. A short usage guide with example notebooks for loading data and computing simple features would lower the barrier further, and a clear license and citation request will help you track reuse.
